messages.subject: Re: BioGeoBears Example Question
parts:
Hi group,

Answering this question:

On Tue, Jul 22, 2014 at 9:37 AM, Bennett Stephens <step...@kenyon.edu> wrote:
Hi Dr. Matzke,

My name is Bennett Stephens, and I am a rising Senior at Kenyon College in Gambier, OH. I am currently doing a summer research project, and am attempting to use the example code provided in the description of the BioGeoBears package. Unfortunately, I seem to be having some problems with the files (I am relatively new to R, so it may be a simple problem!). When you say to set up my working directory as my local system, does that mean to include the files downloaded from the source command above?

The source() commands access .R files at whatever location is specified.  In the example script, to keep it simple, it accesses them from the website.  If one were to download those files and save them in a local directory, you could give source that path+filename and source them locally.

Once you've run the source() commands, you don't have to run them again unless you restart R.

 
I am running into issues farther down the script, where it is not recognizing file names, and I am getting an error stating: " Error in file(con, "r") : cannot open the connection."

This means that R can't find the data files, e.g. your newick tree file, and/or your geography file.  For your own data, you should save those files in some folder somewhere on your computer, and then set your working directory (wd) in the R script with setwd():

wd = "wherever_I_put_the_data_files"
setwd(wd)

To check if setting the wd worked, do:

getwd()

To see if your files are actually in your working directory, do:

list.files()


If you are running just the example script files (Hawaiian Psychotria), these are located inside the BioGeoBEARS R package, and the default script should find them, unless you messed with extdata_dir or something.

I believe the various points above are basically explained in the comments before each command, so restarting R and going through everything line-by-line should help introduce the R basics as well. I would start with just the pure example script.

 
This is followed by the option to "Rerun with debug."

This is an option provided by whatever R application you are running (Rstudio?), it will probably say that any time you hit an error.

Cheers!
Nick

Please also note:

BioGeoBEARS Warnings To Ignore, Mostly
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-warnings-to-ignore-mostly



 
I believe this is a fairly simple problem to fix, but thought I would reach out to see if you knew. Thank you so much for your time!

Sincerely,

H. Bennett Stephens
Kenyon College
Class of 2015
Biology

parts:
Hi! Thanks for the error message.

It's looking for timeperiods.txt, which is a list of times for a time-stratified analysis.  In the example script, the analysis is an unconstrained, non-time-stratified analysis, so the line:

#BioGeoBEARS_run_object$timesfn = "timeperiods.txt"
... is commented out with the "#".

You must have accidentally deleted the "#".  Cheers!

Nick

It's looking for timeperiods.txt, which is a list of times for a time-stratified analysis. In the example script, the analysis is an unconstrained, non-time-stratified analysis, so the line:

You must have accidentally deleted the "#". Cheers!


Nick

On Tue, Jul 22, 2014 at 9:37 AM, Bennett Stephens <step...@kenyon.edu> wrote:


Hi Dr. Matzke,


My name is Bennett Stephens, and I am a rising Senior at Kenyon College in Gambier, OH. I am currently doing a summer research project, and am attempting to use the example code provided in the description of the BioGeoBears package. Unfortunately, I seem to be having some problems with the files (I am relatively new to R, so it may be a simple problem!). When you say to set up my working directory as my local system, does that mean to include the files downloaded from the source command above?


The source() commands access .R files at whatever location is specified. In the example script, to keep it simple, it accesses them from the website. If one were to download those files and save them in a local directory, you could give source that path+filename and source them locally.


Once you've run the source() commands, you don't have to run them again unless you restart R.




I am running into issues farther down the script, where it is not recognizing file names, and I am getting an error stating: " Error in file(con, "r") : cannot open the connection."


This means that R can't find the data files, e.g. your newick tree file, and/or your geography file. For your own data, you should save those files in some folder somewhere on your computer, and then set your working directory (wd) in the R script with setwd():


wd = "wherever_I_put_the_data_files"
setwd(wd)


To check if setting the wd worked, do:


getwd()


To see if your files are actually in your working directory, do:


list.files()




If you are running just the example script files (Hawaiian Psychotria), these are located inside the BioGeoBEARS R package, and the default script should find them, unless you messed with extdata_dir or something.


I believe the various points above are basically explained in the comments before each command, so restarting R and going through everything line-by-line should help introduce the R basics as well. I would start with just the pure example script.




This is followed by the option to "Rerun with debug."


This is an option provided by whatever R application you are running (Rstudio?), it will probably say that any time you hit an error.


Cheers!
Nick
